title: When you guys show teasers or sample shots/vids... are you not worried legally?
author: ericyinglong
selftext:
Do you have an LLC if you plan to release somewhere, or a copyright, and/or a trademark for anything before showing on here or you tube... or anywhere really? 

Do you worry about others taking elements or ideas from you and implementing it into their own project? Or do you get some levels of protection before posting or sharing anything? 

I guess many of these are sub month projects... and not usually longer than 6mo, but for those of you who have or want to share things like that from your games and have spent countless hours and months on it... Anything bad happen ever to you or the project as a result? 

I may just not know the way to proceed legally for sharing or starting a follow along dev YT channel... but this is definitely something I've been thinking a lot about for a steam release especially.

comments.author: Neither_Berry_100
comments.body: From what I understand you can't copy right ai generated content.

replies.author: RuinousFate
replies.body: It's a grey zone. If you make modifications, it becomes not AI content. We'll see this tested in court more though

replies.author: RemarkableWish2508
replies.body:
The AI part is AI and Public Domain (technically "uncopyrightable"). Your templates and your modifications, are yours. Works can have more than one copyright at once, for different parts of the work, and this can never change, the rights can only get sold or licensed.

You don't turn a Public Domain AI output into yours by adding modifications, you get a copyright on your modifications and can manage them any way you want, but anyone is free to pick the base Public Domain stuff (if they can separate both) and use it freely.

replies.author: RuinousFate
replies.body:
I'm simply repeating what the court case around this said. You dont ownly own the modifications.

>***Thaler v. Perlmutter***\*\*:\*\* U.S. courts and the Copyright Office maintain that copyright requires human authorship, and the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear the case in March 2026. Purely AI-generated works cannot be copyrighted in the U.S., though human creative input, arrangement, or substantial edits can qualify for protection.

Source: [https://sites.usc.edu/iptls/2025/02/04/ai-copyright-and-the-law-the-ongoing-battle-over-intellectual-property-rights/](https://sites.usc.edu/iptls/2025/02/04/ai-copyright-and-the-law-the-ongoing-battle-over-intellectual-property-rights/)

Now, it's vague but theoretically if you have creative input in how a character was crafted, you can own it. We have yet to see that tested, however.

No mention of what is public domain or not here nor if a heavily crafted concept counts or not. We'll see these tested over time most likely.

replies.author: RemarkableWish2508
replies.body:
Thaler v. Perlmutter answers a slightly different question: can the AI software, and by extension the maker and/or whoever is executing the AI software, get copyright assigned to it? As in, can OpenAI or Google claim copyright over everything their software generates?

The decision is "no, it can't", which is a really important decision to avoid a dystopian shitstorm... but so far, who can claim a generated output, is most closely decided by the USCO:

* https://www.copyright.gov/ai/

They are being friggin slow with those reports, though.

replies.author: RemarkableWish2508
replies.body:
You're missing some more:

* LLC — holds your reputation, shields you from personal loss... unless you're negligent or run it in bad faith.
* Authorship — always automatically yours, unless you "work for hire".
* Copyright — assigned automatically to you, for everything that you have made yourself. AI part is Public Domain, so you better keep enough of your stuff in the mix.
* Trademark — whatever distinguishable name or tag you use to commercialize stuff under, so people can recognize you. Use it or lose it, not obligatory to register, but recommended.
* Patent — gives you a limited monopoly on inventions, meaning you can stop others from competing with you. Expensive, limited, most software ones are invalid and useless to anyone but large patent trolls.

comments.author: Valdaraak
comments.body:
I say it in every thread this gets mentioned:

People only copy things that are successful.

Nobody here is going to get their shit copied because the idea doesn't have any proven success. Why would a copier target an unproven idea over one that's already shown success?

And also:

>Do you worry about others taking elements or ideas from you and implementing it into their own project? Or do you get some levels of protection before posting or sharing anything?

This isn't a thing. You can't copyright game mechanics or styles. The *presentation* and trade branding can be protected, but not mechanics or general style themselves.

replies.author: Not-a-Clever-UN
replies.body: Except "successful" is measured by audience reach, and several games have already been copied and released before their own release dates, unfortunately.   There was a more recent one, but the one I remember is the needle in a haystack game.

comments.author: Comet7777
comments.body: The bigger worry is that 99% of AI made games won’t even come close to being successful. People only target things that are successful

comments.author: YouKnowItsMeStudios
comments.body:
You don't need an LLC for any of this. An LLC is just a business structure and in no way affects an IP.

The two bigger things that can cover people if they choose to pursue it are "automatic copyright" and "idea-expression dichotomy".

If someone really wanted to pursue legal remedies, what would hold the most ground are your file systems and documents with timestamps and version control history.

If you take x person to court and they show up with an almost exact replica of your game but their history shows it was created two weeks after you posted a video and you have all of your documents showing you've been working on it for six months, that's pretty much a slam dunk.

I'm not a lawyer but that is the jist of it.

comments.author: ipreuss
comments.body: You automatically have copyright for anything copyrightable you create, you don’t need to take any action to “obtain it”.
